cards.b: The band of light across a dark sky is where we look edge-on through our own galaxy. We live inside it, so mapping it is like mapping a forest from within. Learning its shape, size and our place in it was one of the great steps in astronomy.

Galileo saw in 1610 that the Milky Way band breaks into countless faint stars. It is the combined glow of our galaxy's disc, seen from inside. The name Milky Way is old; the Greek word gave us 'galaxy'.

The Milky Way is a barred spiral galaxy: a flat disc about 100,000 light-years across and only about 1,000 thick, a central bulge with a bar of stars, and spiral arms where gas and young stars concentrate. It has roughly 100 to 400 billion stars and a diffuse halo of old stars and globular clusters.

The Sun lies in a minor arm, the Orion Arm (Orion Spur), about 26,000 light-years from the centre. It orbits at about 230 km/s and takes roughly 225 to 250 million years for one lap, a 'galactic year'. Since the Sun formed it has made about 20 laps. The Solar System also bobs up and down through the disc.

cards.h: The centre: a supermassive black hole
cards.b: Dust hides the centre in visible light, but infrared and radio reveal it. Stars at the centre orbit an invisible object, Sagittarius A*, with about 4 million Suns. One star, S2, whips around it every 16 years. In May 2022 the Event Horizon Telescope imaged its shadow.

cards.h: Rotation and a hint of dark matter
cards.b: Stars in the outer disc orbit surprisingly fast, not slowing down with distance as planets in the Solar System do. Visible matter cannot supply enough gravity. That points to a massive halo of dark matter, which holds about 5 to 10 times the mass of all the stars. See lesson 3-0-2.

William Herschel (1785) counted stars and wrongly placed the Sun near the centre. In 1918 Harlow Shapley mapped globular clusters, found that they centre on a point far away in Sagittarius, and so showed that the Sun is off-centre. In 1920 the Shapley-Curtis debate asked if spiral 'nebulae' were separate galaxies; Hubble settled it in 1924 with Cepheids in Andromeda. Gaia now gives 3D positions and motions for nearly two billion stars.

• 'The Milky Way is the universe.' It is one of hundreds of billions of galaxies.
  • 'Stars in the band are all nearby.' The band holds stars up to tens of thousands of light-years away.
  • 'We are at the centre.' We are about halfway out.

The Milky Way and Andromeda will merge in billions of years, though estimates of timing and certainty are being revised.

In Sanskrit and Hindi the Milky Way is Akashganga, the river of the sky, and it appears in many stories. India's GMRT maps the 21 cm hydrogen line to trace gas in spiral arms, and AstroSat studies star clusters across the galaxy in ultraviolet. The lunar nakshatras and the Saptarishi all lie in our local Milky Way neighbourhood.

• The Milky Way is a barred spiral galaxy of 100 to 400 billion stars, about 100,000 light-years across.
  • The Sun is 26,000 light-years from the centre and orbits in about 230 million years.
  • Sgr A*, about 4 million Suns, sits at the centre.
  • Rotation speeds point to a dark matter halo.

Think about it: (1) Why was it so hard to learn our galaxy's shape? (2) What would the sky look like if we lived near the galactic centre?
